The city employed one person to retrieve things that had fallen between the seconds.

Her name was Ada Vale, and her office was beneath the municipal swimming pool. All day, above her ceiling, people practiced not drowning. She found the sound reassuring.

Most losses were small.

A word someone had known until the instant they needed it. The last note of a song, clipped by a train entering a tunnel. The expression on a father’s face when his child, looking elsewhere, said something unexpectedly kind.

These arrived in the pipes.

Ada would hear a tapping, set down her tea, and open the brass valve beside her desk. Whatever had been lost slid into a shallow porcelain basin.

Words resembled fish bones. Musical notes were warm enough to hold against your cheek. Expressions appeared on thin, translucent leaves, which had to be stored flat or they curled into smiles that meant entirely different things.

She catalogued everything.

There were regulations.

Nothing could be returned without proof of ownership. Nothing could be retained for personal use. And no item recovered from between the seconds was to be confused with something deliberately thrown away.

This last rule caused the most arguments.

“Of course I didn’t mean it,” people would say.

Ada would turn the form toward them.

“Then you’ll need to explain what happened.”

One Tuesday, a man brought in an empty shoebox.

“I’ve lost a whole afternoon.”

Ada looked at him over her glasses.

“Have you checked your phone?”

“No. Not that kind.”

He was young enough to think grief had made him old. His coat was buttoned incorrectly, with one side hanging lower than the other. He placed the shoebox on her desk as though something sleeping lay inside.

“My mother’s kitchen,” he said. “Rain against the windows. She was making bread. I was doing homework. Nothing happened.”

“When?”

“Twenty-three years ago.”

“Why do you want it now?”

He looked down.

“She died on Sunday.”

Above them, a whistle blew. Someone shouted, “Again.”

Ada took out a form.

She disliked these cases. Not because they were difficult, although they were. She disliked the way people waited while she searched, watching her hands as if the right movement might undo everything.

“Was there anything distinctive about the afternoon?”

“She kept singing the wrong words.”

“To what?”

“I don’t remember.”

“What kind of bread?”

“I don’t remember.”

“Your homework?”

He shook his head.

Ada pushed the form aside.

“I’ll look.”

After he left, she opened the valve.

A copper taste filled the room. Then came a clatter of misplaced keys, three interrupted sneezes, and the courage a woman had gathered outside a courtroom but dropped before entering.

Ada caught the courage in a jar.

She waited.

The pipes hummed.

By evening, the basin held a chipped blue afternoon.

It was smaller than she expected, no larger than a bar of soap. She lifted it with both hands. Somewhere inside, rain moved down a window, and a boy erased an answer so vigorously that the paper tore.

She should have sealed it immediately.

Instead, she held it a little longer.

The kitchen opened around her.

There was flour on the mother’s sleeve. A radiator knocked under the window. The boy asked whether seven times eight was fifty-four.

“Nearly,” his mother said.

“That means no.”

“It does.”

He sighed and bent over his page.

She sang half a line about a sailor, substituting “cupboard” for a word Ada couldn’t hear. The boy laughed. His mother glanced at him, pleased, then returned to kneading.

That was all.

Ada set the afternoon in a padded envelope.

The man returned the next morning. He had corrected the buttons on his coat.

“I found it,” she said.

His face changed so quickly that she looked away to give him privacy.

“How do I—”

“Hold it. Somewhere quiet. It will last as long as it lasted.”

“Can I go back more than once?”

“No.”

“Can she hear me?”

“No.”

“Can I tell her—”

“No.”

He sat down.

For a while, neither spoke.

Then he asked, “Will it hurt?”

“I don’t know,” Ada said.

He nodded as though this was the first answer he trusted.

She gave him the envelope.

At the door, he stopped.

“Do people ever decide not to?”

“Yes.”

“What happens to those?”

“We keep them.”

“How long?”

Ada glanced toward the shelves behind her desk.

“Until they’re ready.”

That evening, after the swimmers had gone, she took a small parcel from the bottom drawer.

It had been there eleven years.

Inside was a morning at a railway station. Her brother stood beneath the departure board, carrying a green bag. They had argued in the car. When his train was called, she said, “Go, then.”

He went.

She had recovered the moment after the accident, intending to use it straightaway. Then she had learned that he would not hear anything she said. For eleven years, she had kept finding reasons not to open it.

Ada unwrapped the parcel.

The station was cold. Her brother shifted the bag onto his other shoulder.

“Go, then,” she heard herself say.

He looked at her. Tired, annoyed, alive.

Then he reached out and tucked the label of her coat back inside the collar.

“All right,” he said.

She had forgotten that.

The train doors opened.

Ada stayed until the morning ended.
